quantity: Yakaboylu operator constructions (2022-2026): claim history and current statement
statement: v11 of arXiv 2408.15135 (Aug 2025), abstract: 'We demonstrate the existence of a self-adjoint Hamiltonian whose eigenvalues are of the form i(1/2 - rho_s), where rho_s denote the simple nontrivial zeros ... Consequently, all such zeros lie on the critical line.' The current v17 (18 Aug 2026) retreats. R is non-symmetric on L^2([0, inf)), with point spectrum {i(1/2 - lambda) : lambda zero of Gamma(s+1)(1 - 2^{1-s})zeta(s)}. Theorem 3.3 is proved 'assuming the boundary term B[F_s(t)] is suppressed' and then requiring Re(s) > -1. Under the assumption that all zeros are simple, the compressions are intertwined by a symmetric W, and Theorem 4.5 states W > 0 iff Re rho = 1/2 for all simple zeros. W is defined as sum over rho of |Phi_{1-rho-bar}><Phi_rho|, so the equivalence is immediate. The author writes that the self-adjointness of h 'rests on the positivity W > 0; yet this condition already entails Re(rho) = 1/2'. Critique: N. Feldmann (Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.19353727, Mar 2026, preprint) lists three obstructions. (i) The transformed Dirichlet domain is not dense, so the self-adjointness gap is ill-posed. (ii) The bounded positive intertwiner yields only conjugate pairing of eigenvalues, not reality. (iii) The unbounded intertwiner's domain excludes the eigenfunctions. Feldmann also argues that the needed completeness condition is equivalent to the Nyman–Beurling criterion.
value: current version: RH <=> W > 0 (a restatement); the earlier 2025 claim of a self-adjoint realization forcing the simple zeros onto the line has been withdrawn
conditional_on: v17 Theorem 4.5 assumes all nontrivial zeros are simple; Theorem 3.3 assumes a boundary term vanishes

quantity: Other 2024-2026 claimed spectral realizations: what is actually proved
statement: (a) Hedenmalm 2026 (unrefereed). Theorem 3.3.1: for real alpha, the boundary-value problem L D u + alpha L u = 0 on R_>0, with u(0+) = u(inf) = 0 (L built from the Jacobi theta function), has a nonzero solution iff Xi(alpha) = 0, and the solution is unique up to constants, u_alpha. Theorem 4.2.2 and Corollary 4.2.3: if a pair of sesquilinear forms exists, with the second a Hilbert-space inner product, making (L D, L) self-adjoint, then all roots of Xi are real. The existence of such forms is open; the author says it is 'unclear what would be a proper substitute' for a single operator. (b) LeClair–Mussardo (JHEP 2024) and LeClair (ATMP 29 (2025)): Bethe-ansatz energies E_n(sigma) of scattering with impurities equal the zeros in the limit sigma -> 1/2. The S-matrix is built from the Euler product, so an analytic continuation/'thermodynamic limit' is assumed below the region of absolute convergence; the analytic proofs of the spectral-flow Propositions (Section V) assume RH. (c) X.-J. Li 2024 (arXiv 2404.11902): a differential operator on a 'Hilbert–Pólya space' whose eigenvalues are exactly the nontrivial zeros, with explicit eigenfunctions. No self-adjointness is claimed in the abstract, so there is no RH content. (d) Suo, Phys. Rev. A 112 (2025) L060201: a Hamiltonian with E_n = rho_n(1 - rho_n), whose eigenstates are NOT normalizable (the author's own statement). (e) Shi 2026 (arXiv 2609.04908): finite 'Prime–Weil' matrices. The exact-spectrum statement is a reconstruction theorem with the zero ordinates as inputs, and 'assuming RH, lambda_min(S) -> 0'.

quantity: Largest n for which the Li (Keiper–Li) coefficients λ_n have been computed directly from ζ, with no zero input, under rigorous error control
statement: Johansson computes the Keiper–Li coefficients λ_0..λ_n up to n = 100000. The method takes the power series of log ξ(s) = log(−ζ(s)) + log Γ(1+s/2) + log(1−s) − (s/2) log π at s=0 and right-composes it with x/(x−1). ζ is evaluated by Euler–Maclaurin with rigorous error bounds in ball arithmetic (Arb), at a working precision of 1.1n+50 bits, giving about 0.1n accurate bits. Table 2 reports the times 'to determine the signs of λ_n up to n = 1000, 10000 and 100000'. The paper reports λ_100000 = 4.62580782406902231409416038... (Keiper normalization) against Keiper's approximation (1/2)(log n − log 2π + γ − 1) ≈ 4.626132, and says the computation 'shows agreement with Keiper's conjecture (and the Riemann hypothesis)'.
value: λ_n > 0 for all 1 ≤ n ≤ 10^5. λ_100000 (Keiper normalization) = 4.6258078240690223...; Li normalization ≈ 4.6258×10^5.
location: §4.2 'Computing the Keiper-Li coefficients', Table 2 and Figure 1, pp. 9–11 of arXiv v1

caveats: (1) Normalization: Johansson's (Keiper's) λ_n equals Li's λ_n divided by n (Lagarias 2007 §1: Keiper's coefficients = λ_{−n}/n). (2) Positivity is the reported outcome of a ball-arithmetic computation. It is not a numbered theorem, and I found no independent replay. (3) Direct computation in this range carries no new RH information. Zero verification to height T0 already gives λ_n ≥ 0 for n ≤ T0^2 (POS-02). Voros (Exp. Math. 2020, eqs. (17)–(18)) argues that λ_n can detect an off-line zero 1/2+t+iT only for n ≳ T^2/|t| ≳ 2T0^2 ≈ 10^25. (4) Do not confuse this with Voros's deformed sequence Λ_n, which G. Misguich computed (MPFR, not certified) up to n = 5·10^5. (5) McPhedran (arXiv:2311.06294, intro) reports accurate values of the first 4000 coefficients by a different representation.

quantity: Semi-local Li criterion: the range of n for which λ_n ≥ 0 follows from finite zero verification
statement: Oesterlé (2000, unpublished), as quoted by Voros: if Re ρ = 1/2 for all zeros with |Im ρ| ≤ T0, then λ_n ≥ 0 for all n ≤ T0^2. Platt–Trudgian (2021) rigorously verified RH up to T0 = 3·10^12. Together these give λ_n ≥ 0 for all n ≤ 9·10^24; I derived that figure. Voros states ≈5·10^24 using the 2004 height T0 ≈ 2.4·10^12. Oesterlé also proved (unpublished) that under RH λ_n = n((1/2) log n + c) + o(n) with c = (1/2)(γ − log 2π − 1).
value: λ_n ≥ 0 for n ≤ T0^2. With T0 = 3·10^12 this gives n ≤ 9·10^24 (derived; not stated in any source).
conditional_on: Takes as input the rigorous RH verification to height T0 (an established computation, not a hypothesis).
location: Voros arXiv:1703.02844v3, §1, eq. (13) and eq. (14), p. 4; Voros ref. [26]

history.value: asymptotic form valid for n ≤ T^2/(4 log^2 T)

caveats: I found no published proof. Voros calls Oesterlé's typescript 'uncirculated'. Two weaker published semi-local statements exist. (a) Lagarias 2007: RH up to height T implies the finite-place term satisfies the O(√n log n) bound for n ≤ T^2/(4 (log T)^2) (POS-03). (b) Brown 2005 and Palojärvi (POS-05). Brown's converse-type Theorem 2 (zero-free region ⟹ finitely many λ_n ≥ 0) is reported unproved because of an error in his Lemma 5 (Palojärvi, arXiv:1807.01506, §1, citing Droll's thesis). The 9·10^24 figure is arithmetic on the cited theorem plus Platt–Trudgian.

(17)–(18), and ref. [26] 'typescript (2000, revised 2001, uncirculated)'. Platt–Trudgian arXiv:2004.09765 Theorem 1 (height 3 000 175 332 800).
verification.notes: The quote is accurate, and the 'unpublished, secondary' status fits. Two additions. (i) Voros writes that Oesterlé 'proved (but left unpublished [6, §2.3])'. His [6] is Biane–Pitman–Yor, Bull. AMS 38 (2001) 435–465, §2.3, which is an earlier published secondary mention worth citing. (ii) Voros §1.3.2 reproduces 'Oesterlé's argument for the RH true case', which is the asymptotic (14). It does not prove the semi-local (13), so the 'no published proof' caveat stands. The 9·10^24 figure is arithmetic: (3·10^12)^2, or about 9.0·10^24 using H = 3.000175·10^12. quantity: Asymptotics of Li coefficients λ_n (ζ and principal GL(N) automorphic L-functions)
statement: Lagarias, Theorem 1.1. For π irreducible cuspidal unitary on GL(N)/Q and n ≥ 1, unconditionally λ_n(π) = (N/2) n log n + C_1(π) n − λ_n(√n, π) + O(√n log n). Here λ_n(T, π) is the incomplete Li sum over zeros with |Im ρ| < T, and C_1(π) = (N/2)(γ − 1 − log 2π) + (1/2) log Q(π) (eq. (1.13)). Under RH for L(s,π): λ_n(π) = (N/2) n log n + C_1(π) n + O(√n log n) (eq. (1.18)). Two pieces are unconditional: the archimedean part S_∞(n,π) = (N/2) n log n + C_1 n + O(1) (Thm 5.1, eq. (1.12)), and S_f(n,π) = λ_n(√n, π^∨) + O(√n log n) (Thm 6.1). If RH holds up to height T, the O(√n log n) bound for S_f holds for n ≤ T^2/(4 (log T)^2) (p. 4). For ζ: λ_n = (n/2) log n + ((γ − 1 − log 2π)/2) n + O(√n log n) under RH.
value: For ζ under RH: λ_n = (n/2) log n − 1.13033... n + O(√n log n). The constant (γ − 1 − log 2π)/2 ≈ −1.1303307 is computed here.
conditional_on: RH (GRH for L(s,π)) for eq. (1.18). Eqs. (1.12), (1.15)/(6.2) and (1.17) are unconditional.
location: Theorem 1.1 (eqs. (1.12)–(1.18)), Theorem 5.1, Theorem 6.1, pp. 3–4 and §§5–6 of arXiv v4

history.note: heuristic, under a hypothesis stronger than RH

history.value: RH ⟺ λ_n ~ n((1/2) log n + c)
O(√n log n) under GRH, GL(N)

caveats: The O-constants depend on π and are not explicit. Lagarias notes that Keiper's plot suggests |S_f(n)| < 20 for n ≤ 7000, so the true oscillation may be smaller than √n log n; this is unexplained. Voros (MPAG 9 (2006) 53–63) reached the same main terms by the saddle-point method. Voros later records an erratum: an overall minus sign was missed in the RH-false oscillatory term in his 2006/2010 texts. He corrected it in his Kyoto proceedings and says the conclusions are unaffected (Exp. Math. 2020, footnote 1). Selberg-class analogue under GRH: λ_F(n) = (d_F/2) n log n + c_F n + O(√n log n), with c_F = (d_F/2)(γ−1) + (1/2) log(λQ_F^2) (Mazhouda, arXiv:1506.01755; abstract only).

quantity: Sharp asymptotic RH-equivalence via the Keiper–Li sequence
statement: Use Keiper's normalization, log(2ξ(1/s)) = Σ λ_n (1−s)^n, and set y_n = λ_n − (1/2)(log n + γ − log(2πe)). Arias de Reyna proves RH ⟺ (y_n) is square-summable. Voros (2006) proves RH ⟺ n y_n = o(n). If RH fails, λ_n^{Li} ~ −Σ_{Re ρ' > 1/2} z_{ρ'}^{−n}: oscillations of both signs that grow exponentially. Bombieri–Lagarias 1999, Theorem 1(c), already gave the exponential size when RH fails.
value: RH ⟺ Σ_n y_n^2 < ∞
location: Main theorem as given in the zbMATH 5967684 review; Voros, arXiv:1703.02844, eqs. (14)–(16)

quantity: Zero-free regions from finitely many (τ-)Li coefficients (finite-N Li criteria; Dirichlet, Artin and general L-functions)
statement: Brown (2005, Thm 3) treats a class that includes completed Artin L-functions satisfying Artin's conjecture. For that class, Re b_1, ..., Re b_N ≥ 0 for large N implies a certain zero-free region, and Re b_2 ≥ 0 gives a small zero-free region near 1 (a Siegel-zero condition in terms of ξ(1), ξ'(1), ξ''(1)). Palojärvi gives explicit N_1, N_2 for τ-Li coefficients. If Re λ_n^τ ≥ 0 for N_1 ≤ n ≤ N_2, then every zero satisfies |ρ/(ρ−τ)| < R (Thm 3.1). If some Re λ_n^τ < 0 in an explicit range, then some zero has |ρ/(ρ−τ)| ≥ R (Thm 3.3).
value: Qualitative: explicit N_1(R,τ,F) and N_2(R,τ,F), which I did not extract
location: Brown Thm 3 and Cor 1 (from the zbMATH 2208782 review); Palojärvi §1, Theorems 3.1 and 3.3
caveats: Erratum/dispute: according to Palojärvi (§1, citing A. Droll's thesis), Brown's Lemma 5 contains two errors. Droll fixed one; the other leaves Brown's Theorem 2 (zero-free region ⟹ certain λ_n ≥ 0) unproved. I read Palojärvi's introduction only and did not check her constants.

quantity: Largest support window on which Weil's quadratic form is proved positive (published, peer-reviewed)
statement: Connes–Consani, Theorem 1 and Theorem 6.11. Let g ∈ C_c^∞(R_+^*) have support in [2^{−1/2}, 2^{1/2}] and Fourier transform vanishing at i/2. Then W_∞(g*g^*) ≥ Tr(ϑ(g) S ϑ(g)^*) − c|ĝ(0)|^2. Here S is the projection onto the Sonin space, and the best constant satisfies 13 < c < 17 (Remark 6.12). Hence W_∞(f) ≥ 0 for every smooth positive definite f supported in (1/2, 2) whose Fourier transform vanishes at ±i/2 and 0. This is Weil's inequality on a window where no prime contributes, so only the archimedean place enters. The authors write that the result 'was proved in [Yoshida] by reducing it to an explicit computation'. Their contribution is a conceptual proof via compressing the scaling action onto Sonin space, with control by prolate functions and Toeplitz matrices.
value: Test functions supported in [2^{−1/2}, 2^{1/2}]: log half-width (log 2)/2 ≈ 0.3466, autocorrelation support (1/2, 2), no primes
location: Introduction, Theorem 1 and Corollary 2 (pp. 2–3); Theorem 6.11, eq. (141); Remark 6.12 (p. 48ff of arXiv v1)

history.value: RH ⟺ positivity of the quadratic form for all compactly supported test functions
same window, conceptual proof with Sonin trace lower bound

caveats: Attribution nuance: Suzuki (arXiv:2606.09096, §1) cites Yoshida only for positivity of the localized Rayleigh quotient 'for sufficiently small a' (Lemma 2) and for the RH ⟺ non-degeneracy equivalence (Theorem 2). Connes–Consani and Zhu attribute the full (log 2)/2 window to Yoshida. I did not read Yoshida's paper. No prime enters, so this does not test the Euler product. Connes–Consani–Moscovici 2024 (Ann. Funct. Anal. 15, Paper 87, arXiv:2310.18423) builds the semilocal prolate/Sonin framework and proves stability of the semilocal Sonin space, but establishes no new positivity window.

verification.checked_against: Connes–Consani arXiv:2006.13771 v1: intro p. 2 (Theorem 1, eq. (5), Corollary 2, 'This result was proved in [34] by reducing it to an explicit computation'), Theorem 6.11 eq. (141), Remark 6.12 ('best constant… 13 < c < 17'). zbMATH 7383656 (Sel. Math. 27(4), Paper 77, 2021). zbMATH 7935125 (CCM, Ann. Funct. Anal. 15(4), Paper 87, 2024). Suzuki arXiv:2606.09096 §1.
verification.notes: The entry blends two statements. Theorem 1 assumes ĝ vanishes at i/2 and at 0, and gives W∞(g*g*) ≥ Tr(ϑ(g)Sϑ(g)*) with no c-term. Theorem 6.11 assumes vanishing only at −i/2, and the bound carries −c|ĝ(0)|^2 with c = 4γ/log 2. Here γ is a constant from Lemma 6.10, not Euler's constant, and the best c lies in (13, 17). The derived W∞(f) ≥ 0 for positive-definite f supported in (1/2, 2), with f̂ vanishing at ±i/2 and 0, is stated in the paper. The CCM title is 'Zeta zeros and prolate wave operators: semilocal adelic operators'.

quantity: Certified Weil positivity on windows that contain primes: half-width L of supp f in the log variable
statement: Zhu, Theorem 1.2. For every real even f ∈ L^2(R) with supp f ⊆ [−0.8, 0.8], Q(f) ≥ 8.9×10^{−18} ||f||_2^2, so the Weil form is positive on all autocorrelations g = f⋆f̃ with supp g ⊆ [−1.6, 1.6]. Corollary 6.3 extends this to arbitrary complex f: the odd sector is certified with Q ≥ 8.2×10^{−15}. Theorem 6.2 states that the window ground state is simple and even. A certified variational upper bound gives λ*(0.8) ≤ 2.27×10^{−17}; upper bounds decay to 3.2×10^{−283} at L = 2. Theorem 1.3 (under RH): λ*(L) ≤ exp(−L e^L) for L ≥ L0. Theorem 1.4 (unconditional barrier): every certificate built on the one-stroke reduction needs T♯ > 2π e^{A_L} with A_L = (4+o(1)) e^L. The matrix size therefore grows doubly exponentially in L, and no pointwise bound on the prime comb can lower this threshold.
value: L = 0.8, about 2.3 times the classical (log 2)/2. Autocorrelation window [e^{−1.6}, e^{1.6}] ≈ [0.202, 4.953], so the prime powers 2, 3 and 4 enter. Enclosure 8.9×10^{−18} ≤ λ*(0.8) ≤ 2.27×10^{−17}.
location: Theorems 1.1–1.4 (pp. 3–5), Theorem 6.2, Corollary 6.3, §5 (certificate), §7 (exploratory L=1.19), §§12–14
caveats: Self-correction: an earlier draft claimed a certified theorem at support 2.38 (L = 1.19). It relied on a per-prime 'sharpening' of the envelope that bounds the prime comb in the wrong direction (Remark 3.3; Lemma 3.2 shows no such sharpening exists), and the claim is retracted. L = 1.19 survives only as exploratory evidence: a 950×950 matrix at 70 digits with λ_min ∈ (10^{−48}, 10^{−46}). The certificate uses 50-digit precision, Bernstein-ellipse quadrature, a tail bound and a verified Cholesky residual. I found no independent replay. The law −ln λ*(L) ≈ 2π^2 N(T*)/ln N(T*) with T* = 2πe^{2L} is fitted to upper bounds (C = 20.13...) and is not proved (Conjecture 12.1). The paper also warns that float64 evaluation of the geometric side produces spurious negative eigenvalues. Normalization: the classical window is L = (log 2)/2.

verification.checked_against: Zhu arXiv:2608.24827 v2 full text: abstract; Theorems 1.1–1.4 (pp. 3–5); Remarks 1.5–1.6; Lemma 3.2; Remark 3.3; threshold table (L = 0.8 → T1 = 119; L = 1.19 → 7.4×10^3); §5 certificate (T♯ = 200, N = 200, 50 digits, margin 10^−19); eq. (14) odd sector 8.2065×10^−15; Theorem 6.2; Corollary 6.3; §7 (retraction and the corrected L = 1.19 cost); eq. (5) with C = 20.13.
verification.notes: All constants match. The status (unrefereed, no independent replay) is right. One omission matters for the frontier. Zhu §7 already works out what an honest L = 1.19 certificate needs. A direct scan shows the actual symbol Ψ_L, not only the envelope, dips below β* by about 2 near t ≈ 1550, with the last dip at t0 ≈ 8.48×10^3. A valid certificate therefore needs T♯ ≳ 8.5×10^3, which is certifiable by adaptive interval evaluation of Ψ_L, and N ≈ 1.4–2×10^4 Legendre orders at about 90 digits. Zhu calls this 'roughly three orders of magnitude more work' and says it was 'not carried out'. The record should cite this.

quantity: Weil quadratic form QW_λ on [λ^{−1}, λ]: numerical lowest eigenvalue, real-rootedness of the ground state, and conditional positivity
statement: Andrews–Connes–La Gatta. Let QW_λ^N be the Galerkin truncation. If its lowest eigenvalue is simple and its eigenvector is even under u ↦ u^{−1}, then the Mellin transform of the ground state has only real zeros. This is an unconditional theorem (their Theorem 7.1, quoting [8, Thm 5.6]). Numerically, at λ^2 = 250 (53 primes) and N = 4000, those zeros reproduce the first 1000 zeta zeros to more than 500 decimals, the first one to 1341 decimals, and all 2469 zeros up to height 3000 to at least 12 digits. A certified ball-arithmetic sign count shows the finite transform has no other zero in that range. The lowest eigenvalue is ≈1.1·10^{−1346} there and ~10^{−1618} at λ^2 = 300, and is observed to be simple, isolated and even. Theorem 8.14 proves positivity of QW_λ on an explicitly conditioned finite-codimension subspace, assuming hypothesis (H2′). With monotonicity in λ, this reduces positivity of QW_λ to a two-sided Schur-complement estimate on O(log λ) edge modes and two pole directions.
value: Numerically observed: QW_λ^N > 0 up to λ^2 = 300, with ε_λ(1) ~ 10^{−1618}
conditional_on: Theorem 8.14 assumes (H2′); the convergence estimates assume the Fuchs-ladder hypothesis (Hyp. 3.4) and positivity of QW_λ.
location: Abstract; §1 (pp. 3–4); §4 'Eigensolver' (p. 15–16); Theorem 7.1; Theorem 8.14; §9 open items

history.value: low-lying zeros from QW_λ on small windows

caveats: (1) The eigenvalues are not certified. At λ^2 = 100 the Arb ball radii are 'meaningless' (condition number ≈ 10^529), so the iteration runs on midpoints with residual control. (2) A positive lowest eigenvalue of a Galerkin truncation bounds the infimum of QW_λ from above. It is not a lower certificate, and positivity of QW_λ on any window containing primes is not established here (contrast POS-07). (3) Only the upper bound ε_λ(j) ≤ C_j δ_{4j}(λ)(log λ)^3 is proved (with Kastoris); the lower bound is tested numerically. (4) Minor discrepancy: the first-zero accuracy at λ^2 = 13 is 2.6×10^{−55} in Connes's 2026 survey abstract (arXiv:2602.04022) and 2.4×10^{−55} in the ACLG introduction. (5) Groskin (arXiv:2607.02828) gives a certification rule: finite-cutoff negative eigenvalues in the band [−B_T, 0) certify nothing.

quantity: Jensen polynomials J^{d,n} of ξ: largest degree d for which hyperbolicity is known for all shifts n ≥ 0
statement: Chasse's criterion, generalized in GORTTW Theorem 1.2: if RH_m(T) holds (zeros of ξ^{(m)} with |Im| ≤ T lie on the line) and d ≤ ⌊T⌋^2, then J^{d,n} is hyperbolic for all n ≥ m. Platt's verification to T = 3.06·10^10 gives GORTTW Corollary 1.3: J^{d,n} is hyperbolic for d ≤ 9.36·10^20 and all n ≥ 0. Ono (2026) applies Platt–Trudgian's 3·10^12 to get hyperbolicity for every d ≤ 9·10^24. The non-zero-verification route remains d ≤ 3: Csordas–Norfolk–Varga for d = 2 and Dimitrov–Lucas for d = 3. GORZ Theorem 2 (d ≤ 8, all n) was a computer-assisted 'sketch'.
value: d ≤ 9·10^24, all n ≥ 0 (using Platt–Trudgian T = 3·10^12)
location: GORTTW Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3 (p. 2, arXiv v3); Ono 2026, §1, p. 2 (paragraph before Theorem 1)

GORZ's footnote states it only for J^{d,0}; GORTTW states it for all n ≥ 0. (3) GORZ Theorem 2 (d ≤ 8) is a 'Sketch of the Proof' (§5.2): hyperbolicity was checked by Hermite's criterion for n ≤ 10^6 with no stated rigor contract, and it is subsumed by the zero-verification route. The zbMATH review of the journal version reads: 'if d ≤ 9×10^24 and n ≥ 0, then J^{d,n}(X) is hyperbolic'. Ono 2026 only restates it, so the record is GORTTW 2022 (Chasse's criterion plus Platt–Trudgian), not Ono 2026. The 9.36×10^20 figure belongs to arXiv v3 only. Update value attribution, source and history.
verification.notes: The rest is right. The Chasse figure is 10^17 per zbMATH and 2×10^17 per GORZ and GORTTW. GORZ's footnote applies to J^{d,0} only. GORZ Theorem 2 (d ≤ 8) is a sketch: Hermite's criterion checked for n ≤ 10^6 with no stated rigor contract. Since the zbMATH reading comes from the review, check the published Corollary against the journal PDF before final integration.

quantity: Shift threshold N(d) beyond which J^{d,n} is hyperbolic (each fixed degree d)
statement: GORZ Theorem 1: for each d ≥ 1, J^{d,n} is hyperbolic for all sufficiently large n, via the Hermite-polynomial limit (Theorem 3; ineffective). GORTTW Theorem 1.1: there is an absolute constant c > 0 such that J^{d,n} is hyperbolic for d ≥ 1 and n ≥ c·e^{d/2}. Kim–Lee Theorem 1: if f is a transcendental real entire function of order ρ < 2 with zeros in the strip |Im z| < 1/2, then N(f; d) = O(d^{c/2}) for every c > ρ. For Ξ_0 this gives N(Ξ_0; d) = O(d^c) for every c > 1/2, i.e. hyperbolicity for n ≫_ε d^{1/2+ε}. Holland 2026 (Theorem 1.1): there is an absolute K > 0 such that n^3 log^2(n+2) ≥ K d^5 implies J^{d,n} has d distinct negative real zeros. His Theorem 1.2 adds a joint semicircle law along such (n,d) sequences.
value: N(d) = O_ε(d^{1/2+ε}) (Kim–Lee, ineffective constant). Explicit-shape alternatives: n ≥ c e^{d/2} (GORTTW) and n ≳ d^{5/3}/log^{2/3} (Holland 2026).
location: Kim–Lee Theorem 1 and Theorems 2–3 (pp. 1–2 of arXiv v1); GORTTW Theorem 1.1 and the end of §2.2 (n ≥ α_C d^{13/3}(1+√(1+16C^2))^{d/3} ≤ c e^{d/2}); GORZ Theorems 1 and 3; Holland Theorems 1.1–1.2

history.note: unrefereed; weaker region, adds semicircle law

caveats: (1) Kim–Lee remark that their proof 'gives no information about the Jensen polynomials considered, except that they are hyperbolic'. Their theorem holds for every real entire function of order < 2 with zeros in a strip, including functions that violate RH, so large-shift hyperbolicity cannot encode RH (POS-18). (2) The constants c in GORTTW and K in Holland are absolute but not computed numerically. (3) Holland 2026 does not cite Kim–Lee. For hyperbolicity alone his region (n ≳ d^{5/3}) is weaker than Kim–Lee's (n ≳ d^{1/2+ε}); his new content is distinctness, the explicit power shape and the joint semicircle limit. Ono 2026 also calls Kim–Lee 'the present best result'. (4) Other L-functions: Wagner (Forum Math. 2020, arXiv:1905.11269) proved fixed-degree, large-shift hyperbolicity for Dedekind zeta functions (per Ono 2026; not read).

quantity: Unshifted Jensen polynomials J_d = J^{d,0} as d → ∞: number of real zeros
statement: Ono 2026, Theorem 1: there is an absolute constant C > 0 such that for each d ≥ 2, J_d(X) has at least d − C√d log d distinct negative real roots, so the proportion of real zeros tends to 1 with error O(√(log d/d)). Theorem 3 gives the analogue for the Dedekind zeta function of any number field K: J_{K,d} is nonzero and has at least d − C_K √d log d distinct negative real zeros for d ≥ d_0(K).
value: #real zeros ≥ d − C√d log d
location: Theorem 1, Remark 2, Theorem 3, Remark 4 (pp. 1–3)

history.value: d − O(√d log d) real roots

caveats: Remark 4 (author): the estimate 'does not rule out zeros of ζ_K(s) off the critical line' and 'does not yield a new zero-free region or zero-density estimate'. RH needs the error term to be zero for every d. The abstract says the main theorems were 'autoformalized in Lean 4 by AxiomProver'; I did not inspect the formalization. C is not numerically explicit.

quantity: Turán and higher-order Turán inequalities for the Taylor/moment coefficients of ξ
statement: Csordas–Norfolk–Varga 1986. With ξ(x/2) = 8∫_0^∞ Φ(t) cos(xt) dt and b_m = ∫_0^∞ t^{2m} Φ(t) dt, the Turán inequalities b_m^2 > ((2m−1)/(2m+1)) b_{m−1} b_{m+1} hold for every m ≥ 1, solving Pólya's 1927 question. The proof shows that K(t) = ∫_t^∞ Φ(√u) du is strictly log-concave for t > 0. Dimitrov–Lucas 2011: the higher-order Turán inequalities hold for all indices, which is equivalent to hyperbolicity of the degree-3 Jensen polynomials for every shift.
value: d = 2 and d = 3 inequalities, for all indices
location: Main theorems, as given in zbMATH 3971145 and 5870997
caveats: These are necessary conditions of RH only. GORZ note that these works use a slightly different normalization of γ(n). Both are subsumed in degree range by the zero-verification route (POS-09), but they do not consume zero verification in the same way. I did not open either full text.

quantity: Pólya-frequency (Toeplitz-minor) and infinite log-concavity properties of the ξ coefficient sequence
statement: Michalowski 2026, Theorem 1.1: for the normalized positive coefficient sequence (a_k) of ξ, the consecutive Toeplitz minors D_{r,k} = det[a_{k+j−i}]_{i,j<r} satisfy D_{r,k} > 0 for every r ≥ 2 and every k ≥ 10^18 r^3. The constants are certified with directed rounding in Arb and exact rational checks, and no zero verification is used. Background stated there (§1.2): Csordas–Norfolk–Varga gives D_{2,k} > 0 for all k. Katkova (2007) shows D_{m,k} > 0 for k ≥ N(m) with no explicit N(m). Schoenberg's sector theorem plus Platt–Trudgian's height H = 3,000,175,332,800 gives D_{r,k} ≥ 0 for all k whenever r ≤ ⌊πH⌋ − 1 ≈ 9.4·10^12. Liu–Mao 2026, Theorem 1.1: for F(x) = ξ(1/2+√x) = Σ λ_n x^n, (L^m λ)_n > 0 for all m, n ≥ 0, i.e. the sequence is strictly infinitely log-concave. This resolves Zhu's conjecture; Zhu (Math. Z. 2023) had proved 6-log-concavity.
value: D_{r,k} > 0 for k ≥ 10^18 r^3 (all r). PF_r for r ≤ ≈9.4·10^12 via verified zeros. Infinite log-concavity unconditional (unrefereed).
location: Michalowski Theorem 1.1, Remark 1.2, §1.2 (pp. 1–2); Liu–Mao Theorem 1.1 (p. 3)

history.value: fixed m: D_{m,k} > 0 for k ≥ N(m); ξ_1 ∈ PF_43

caveats: Michalowski, Remark 1.2: the result covers only the tail regime k ≥ 10^18 r^3 and 'makes no progress on the Riemann Hypothesis'. The RH-critical regime is k ~ r, and the region k < 10^18 r^3 'remains completely open'. RH ⟺ (a_k) is PF_∞ (Aissen–Schoenberg–Whitney–Edrei). Infinite log-concavity is only a necessary consequence of RH (Brändén 2011). Katkova's zbMATH summary records ξ_1 ∈ PF_43 (Comput. Methods Funct. Theory 7 (2007) 13–31), far below the sector-theorem bound. Do not confuse Liu–Mao's λ_n (Taylor coefficients) with Li coefficients.

Schoenberg's rule (zeros avoid |arg| < πm/(m+1) ⟹ PF_m) gives m = 43, so PF43 is the consistent value. The arXiv figure is an off-by-one. The sector-theorem PF_r bound for r ≲ 9.4·10^12 is a direct corollary stated in a preprint, not a separately published theorem. The 'announced_unrefereed' status fits the two 2026 results only.

quantity: Laguerre inequalities for Ξ (Csordas–Varga-type criteria) and Pólya-frequency order of the reciprocal densities
statement: The global Laguerre inequality L_1[Ξ](x) = Ξ'(x)^2 − Ξ(x)Ξ''(x) ≥ 0 for all real x remains open (Csordas 1998, Problem 2); Sra 2026 states this explicitly. Sra, Theorem 1.3: if all zeros with 0 < γ ≤ T (T > 1/2) are on the line, then L_n[Ξ](x) ≥ 0 for every n ≥ 0 and |x| ≤ T − 1/2. Here L_n[f] is the coefficient of y^{2n} in |f(x+iy)|^2, and the n = 1 case is Csordas–Ruttan–Varga 1991. Sra, Theorem 1.2: let Θ and Λ be the densities with one-sided Laplace transform 1/(c_0 ξ(1/2+√s)) and bilateral Laplace transform 1/Ξ. Both are strictly log-concave (PF_2) unconditionally, using zeros only up to height 100. Using verification through height 3,000,175,332,800, both are PF_{k*} with k* = 1,810,540,931,075. Conversely, a pole obstruction gives: PF_k implies every zero below the (k+2)-nd lies on the line. Under RH both densities are PF_∞ (Schoenberg; Gröchenig 2020), and that property is equivalent to RH.
location: Summary items (1)–(3) and Theorems 1.1–1.3 (pp. 1–3)

history.value: necessary and sufficient conditions (Laguerre-type) for RH
all L_n on the verified interval; PF_{k*} of 1/Ξ density

caveats: The author calls these 'merely weak necessary conditions' that do not extend the verified height. The interval Laguerre results are corollaries of zero verification, like POS-09. Csordas–Varga 1990 (Adv. Appl. Math. 11, 328–357) gives the underlying necessary-and-sufficient criteria; I did not read it (zbMATH review unavailable). Related unrefereed 2026 claim: Planat–Solé (arXiv:2608.19160) prove the Csordas–Dimitrov conjecture (Csordas 2015 Open Problem 4.14) that log(s'^2 − s s'') is strictly concave for s(t) = Φ(√t), with computer-assisted certificates; abstract only.

Planat–Solé 2608.19160 metadata.

quantity: Pólya universal factors and the de Bruijn–Newman constant Λ (heat-flow deformation of the Φ kernel)
statement: Following Pólya's universal factors, de Bruijn showed that e^{λu^2}, λ > 0, is a universal factor. Newman's constant Λ is defined so that H_t(x) = ∫_0^∞ e^{tu^2} Φ(u) cos(xu) du has only real zeros exactly when t ≥ Λ, and RH ⟺ Λ ≤ 0. Rodgers–Tao proved Newman's conjecture Λ ≥ 0. Upper bounds: the Polymath abstract records Λ < 1/2 (Ki–Kim–Lee), and Polymath itself obtains a new upper bound (0.22 from memory, abstract truncated). Platt–Trudgian Λ ≤ 0.2 is from memory. Unrefereed 2026 claims: Λ < 0.156821 (computer-assisted collision exclusion, arXiv:2611.06245), and Λ ≤ 0.13963 assuming no zeros with Re s > 7/8 (arXiv:2610.12803). Michalowski 2026 (arXiv:2602.20313 v2) certifies that the kernel K(u) = Φ(|u|) is not PF_5: an explicit 5×5 Toeplitz minor lies in [−1.8472496×10^{−9}, −1.8472225×10^{−9}].
value: 0 ≤ Λ ≤ 0.2 (published, memory). Claimed: Λ < 0.156821 (2026, unrefereed).
location: Main theorem (abstract)
caveats: This is a neighbouring area; the details belong to the de Bruijn–Newman ledger. Λ ≥ 0 is the main negative result for heat-flow and universal-factor approaches: RH, if true, holds with no positive-time slack. Michalowski v2 withdrew the 'certified global sign and unique-threshold claims for C_5' made in v1 because the derivative-tail enclosure was unsound; the PF_5 counterexample stands. Not being PF_5 concerns total positivity of Φ itself and does not bear on RH directly. The PF_∞ criterion concerns the density with transform 1/Ξ (POS-14). The Platt–Trudgian and Polymath numerical bounds were not re-opened here.

verification.checked_against: Rodgers–Tao arXiv:1801.05914 v5 intro (history paragraph and Table 1). zbMATH 7195894 (Forum Math. Pi 8 (2020) e6). Metadata for 2611.06245 (Planat, Raymond), 2610.12803 (Hakimoglu-Brown), 2602.20313 v2 (Michalowski).

Rodgers–Tao state it this way: 'From results of Pólya… if Ht has purely real zeroes… then Ht′… for all t′ > t. De Bruijn showed… t ≥ 1/2'. Replace the 'memory' items with verified ones: Polymath Λ ≤ 0.22 (Res. Math. Sci. 6 (2019), arXiv:1904.12438); Platt–Trudgian Λ ≤ 0.2 (arXiv:2004.09765 §3.4; journal venue Bull. LMS 53 (2021) not re-checked here); Ki–Kim–Lee Λ < 1/2; Rodgers–Tao venue Forum Math. Pi 8 (2020) e6 confirmed.

The latter assumes no zeros with Re s > 7/8, 'as asserted in a recent unrefereed preprint of OpenAI'. Flag that hypothesis as an unverified claim, not an established input. Planat–Raymond themselves mention other recent unrefereed bounds; Planat also has 2609.37164, 2610.18214 and 2610.32694. Those belong in the DBN ledger. The Michalowski v2 withdrawal is confirmed.

quantity: Nyman–Beurling–Báez-Duarte distance d_N: lower bound and conditional asymptotic
statement: Burnol, Theorem 1.3, improving Báez-Duarte–Balazard–Landreau–Saias (Theorem 1.2: Σ 1/|ρ|^2): liminf_{λ→0} D(λ)·√log(1/λ) ≥ √(Σ_ρ m_ρ^2/|ρ|^2). Here D(λ) is the Nyman–Beurling distance, distinct zeros on the line are counted once, and m_ρ is the multiplicity. The bound is unconditional and trivial if RH fails. In Báez-Duarte's discrete form: liminf d_N^2 log N ≥ Σ m(ρ)^2/|ρ|^2. Under RH, Σ m(ρ)/|ρ|^2 = 2 + γ − log 4π. Bettin–Conrey–Farmer, Theorem 1: assume RH and Σ_{|Im ρ| ≤ T} 1/|ζ'(ρ)|^2 ≪ T^{3/2−δ}. Then for V_N(s) = Σ_{n≤N} (1 − log n/log N) μ(n) n^{−s}, (1/2π)∫|1 − ζV_N(1/2+it)|^2 dt/(1/4+t^2) ~ (2+γ−log 4π)/log N. This matches Burnol's lower bound.
value: d_N^2 ~ (2+γ−log 4π)/log N ≈ 0.04620/log N (conditional; constant computed here). Unconditional: liminf d_N^2 log N ≥ Σ m_ρ^2/|ρ|^2.
conditional_on: RH, plus Σ_{|Im ρ|≤T} |ζ'(ρ)|^{−2} ≪ T^{3/2−δ}, which implicitly forces simple zeros. Gonek/Hughes–Keating–O'Connell predict ~ (6/π^3) T.
location: BCF Theorem 1 and the display before it (p. 2); Burnol Theorems 1.2–1.3 (pp. 3–4) and Theorem 5.5
caveats: Only the lower bound is unconditional; an unconditional d_N → 0 would be RH. Convergence is at best logarithmic, so finite computations of d_N cannot quantitatively approach RH. Báez-Duarte's strengthening (RH ⟺ χ ∈ closure of span{ρ_a : a ∈ N}; arXiv:math/0202141) is an equivalence only.

quantity: Horizontal monotonicity of |ξ|, |ζ|, |η| (Sondow–Dumitrescu-type criteria)
statement: Sondow–Dumitrescu 2010: |ξ| is strictly increasing along every horizontal half-line in any open right half-plane containing no zeros of ξ, and decreasing in zero-free left half-planes. Hence |ξ| is monotone for σ ≥ 1 (σ ≤ 0) unconditionally, and monotonicity on σ ≥ 1/2 (σ ≤ 1/2) is equivalent to RH (MSZ Corollary 2.5, implicit in Pólya 1927, and in Lagarias 1999 / Hinkkanen 1997 via Re ξ'/ξ > 0). Matiyasevich–Saidak–Zvengrowski: for |t| ≥ 8 and σ < 1/2, Re η'/η < Re ζ'/ζ < Re ξ'/ξ (Thm 1.3). Consequently |η|, |ζ| and |ξ| are monotone decreasing in σ on σ ≤ 0, |t| ≥ 8 (Thm 1.4). The conclusion fails for |t| < 6.2897 for ζ and η, and extending it to σ ≤ 1/2 is equivalent to RH.
value: Unconditional on σ ≤ 0 (|t| ≥ 8 for ζ, η; all t for ξ). The strip 0 < σ < 1/2 is open (⟺ RH).
location: MSZ Theorems 1.1, 1.3, 1.4, Corollary 2.5 and Theorem 3.4 (pp. 2–5, arXiv v1); SD main theorem (zbMATH 5881207)
caveats: The unconditional range is exactly where zero-freeness is already known. Any extension into 0 < σ < 1/2 on full half-lines is a zero-free-region statement. Related partial results by Goldštein–Grigutis (arXiv:2201.08599) and Grigutis–Turčinskas (arXiv:2509.18963) on Re ξ'/ξ > 0 near the line bound only the contribution of on-line zeros, so they do not exclude off-line zeros. Abstract only.

quantity: Negative/meta result: the Jensen-polynomial route and its information content
statement: Farmer argues, with explicit examples, that hyperbolicity of Jensen polynomials is a universal phenomenon unrelated to RH. Ki's theorem gives lim (−1)^n A_n Ξ^{(2n)}(C_n z) = cos z, and it holds in the extended Selberg class, which contains functions violating RH. Kim's theorem says all zeros of f^{(n)} in |z| < R are real for large n. Chasse's theorem shows that J^{d,0} disperses zero information. Example: X_10(z) = cos z·(z^2−(10+i)^2)(z^2−(10−i)^2)/((z^2−(5π/2)^2)(z^2−(7π/2)^2)) has non-real zeros, yet J^{d,0}_{X_10} has only real zeros for d ≤ 118 and non-real zeros for all larger d. Table 4.1 gives 118, 749, 1897, 4242 for j = 10, 20, 40, 60. The Taylor polynomial detects the violation already at d ≥ 20, 60, 118, 175.
value: X_10: real-rooted J^{d,0} up to d = 118 despite an off-line zero at height ≈ 10
location: §2 (Theorem 2.1, Ki), §4.2 and Table 4.1 (pp. 3, 8–9 of arXiv v2)
caveats: The table values come from Mathematica computations with no stated rigor. The conclusion that the approach is 'not plausible' is an argued heuristic, not a theorem. It is reinforced by Kim–Lee (POS-10), whose large-shift theorem holds for any order-<2 real entire function with zeros in a strip, and by Ono 2026, Remark 4. GORTTW Remark (3) independently calls a converse influence 'highly unlikely' unless hyperbolicity holds for all n and all d.

source.title: Jensen polynomials are not a plausible route to proving the Riemann Hypothesis

verification.checked_against: Farmer arXiv:2008.07206 v2: Theorem 2.1 (Ki); the extended-Selberg-class and random-function remarks; X10 definition; 'J^{d,0}_{X10,cl} has only real zeros for d ≤ 118'; Table 4.1 (118/749/1897/4242; 20/60/118/175). zbMATH 7629539 (Adv. Math. 411, Part A, 108781 (2022)).
verification.notes: Add Farmer's sharper point. For X10, every derivative has only real zeros, so the classical J^{d,n} is real-rooted for all n ≥ 1 and all d even though the 'RH' fails. That alone shows that hyperbolicity for all positive shifts carries no RH information. Table values come from Mathematica, with no rigor claimed. Farmer's ratio d_max/j² ≈ 1.2 supports the frontier's f(D) ≈ c√D.

quantity: Variational structure of the localized Weil form: existence of minimizers, continuity in the window, eigenvalue counts
statement: Bombieri 2000. The infimum of T(f*f̄^*) is attained on the unit sphere of L^2 functions supported in [−t, t]. In W_0^{1,2}([M^{−1}, M]), if the infimum is negative it is attained. For finite truncations: if RH fails with only finitely many off-line zeros, then for large enough truncations the number of negative eigenvalues equals half the number of off-line zeros. Suzuki 2026, Theorem 1.3, proves without RH that the lowest eigenvalue λ_a of the localized form on (−a, a) is continuous in a, with no parity restriction. Since λ_a > 0 for small a, this gives another proof of Yoshida's equivalence: RH ⟺ non-degeneracy for every a.

quantity: Montgomery form factor F(alpha) on |alpha| <= 1 (zeta, assuming RH)
statement: Assume RH. Define F(alpha,T) = (T log T/2pi)^{-1} sum_{0<gamma,gamma'<=T} T^{i alpha(gamma-gamma')} w(gamma-gamma') with w(u)=4/(4+u^2). Then F is real, even and nonnegative, and F(alpha,T) = (T^{-2|alpha|} log T + |alpha|)(1 + O(sqrt(log log T/log T))) uniformly for 0 <= |alpha| <= 1. Montgomery (1973) proved this for |alpha| <= 1-eps; Goldston-Montgomery (1987, Lemma 8) extended it to the closed range with this error term. Consequence: the pair correlation of normalized ordinates agrees with 1-(sin pi u/pi u)^2 for test functions whose Fourier transform is supported in [-1,1]. Montgomery's strong conjecture F(alpha) ~ 1 for |alpha| >= 1, uniformly on bounded sets, is open.

quantity: Average of F(alpha) over long intervals; equivalent forms of the pair correlation conjecture
statement: Assume RH. For b >= 1 and large ell: 0.9303 + o(1) < (1/ell) int_b^{b+ell} F(alpha,T) d alpha < 1.3208 + o(1) as T -> infinity. The upper bound is uniform in b; the lower bound needs ell >= ell0(b). Thm 1 gives 1 + c0(C1-1) and C1 with c0 = min sin x/x = -0.217233... and C1 < 1.3208. Under GRH (Cor. 4) the bounds are 0.9314 and 1.3155. For the GRH Dirichlet family (Cor. 6) they are 0.9858 and 1.0650. Equivalences under RH (as listed by Carneiro-Chandee-Chirre-Milinovich, from Gallagher-Mueller, Goldston, and Goldston-Gonek-Montgomery): Montgomery's PCC for each fixed beta is equivalent to each of (II) int_b^{b+ell} F ~ ell for all fixed b >= 1, ell > 0; (III) Selberg's prime-variance integral J(beta,T) ~ (beta - 1/2) log^2 T / T for fixed beta > 1; (IV) I(a,T) ~ ((1-e^{-2a})/(4a^2)) T log^2 T for fixed a > 0 (second moment of zeta'/zeta near the line). Goldston-Montgomery (1987): the strong PCC is equivalent to an asymptotic for the second moment of primes in short intervals.

statement: Assume RH. Let K_n be the band-limited Schwartz functions eta on R^n with Fourier support in {xi : xi_1+...+xi_n != 0 or |xi_1|+...+|xi_n| < 2}. statement: There is a deterministic sequence {c_j} of real points with c_{j+1} - c_j in {1/2, 1, 3/2, 2, ...} for all j. statement: (a) Bondarenko-Heap: Assume RH. Then mu <= 1/2. The proof assumes 1/2 < c < min(1,mu), so that each short interval holds at most one zero. It bounds |F| <= 1 + 6pi/log T for F(s) = -i [e^{i pi(c-1/2)} zeta(s+i pi c/log T) - zeta(s-i pi c/log T)]/[e^{i pi(c-1/2)} zeta(s+i pi c/log T) + zeta(s-i pi c/log T)], then gets a contradiction by Mobius resonance of length T^{1/(2c)}. (b) Durkan-Pearce-Crump, Thm 1: unconditionally mu <= 1/2 for every fixed primitive Dirichlet character chi; conductor Q=1 is zeta. Infinitely many off-line zero pairs share ordinates and force mu=0; otherwise all high zeros lie on the line and a moment argument (all fixed moments of a shifted log-difference, weighted by a Mobius polynomial) applies. (c) Inoue: under RH mu < 0.50895 (proof gives 0.508949), by a 'resonance-correlation' method based on N_h(t)^2 - N_h(t). Lamzouri (2611.14486, footnote 1) remarks that the Inoue and Bondarenko-Heap results also hold unconditionally by the same dichotomy.

quantity: Proven limitations of the Montgomery-Odlyzko (MO) criterion (negative results)
statement: MO criterion: with h(c) = c - Re sum_{kn<=y} a_k conj(a_{kn}) g(n) Lambda(n)/n^{1/2} / sum |a_k|^2 and y = T^{1-delta}, h(c) > 1 gives mu <= c and h(c) < 1 gives lambda >= c (under RH). Correcting a CGG misprint, MO also cannot prove lambda >= 5.5602 or, with a refinement, lambda >= 3.6747. (iii) Inoue-Kobayashi-Toma: for every coefficient sequence and length L <= T, MO is limited to mu1 >= 0.508 and lambda1 <= 3.022.

quantity: Positive proportion of small gaps under RH: smallest lambda with D(lambda) > 0
statement: D(lambda) := liminf N(T)^{-1} #{gamma_n <= T : gamma_{n+1}-gamma_n <= 2pi lambda/log T}. Durkan-Pearce-Crump, Thm 2: assume RH for zeta. For every eps>0 there is c_eps>0 such that #{n : T <= gamma_n <= gamma_{n+1} <= 2T, (gamma_{n+1}-gamma_n) log gamma_n/2pi < 1/2+eps} >= c_eps T log T. So D(lambda) > 0 for every lambda > 1/2. Previous refereed record: Bui-Goldston-Milinovich-Montgomery (Acta Arith. 210 (2023) 133-153), D(lambda) > 0 for lambda > 0.6039 under RH.
value: RH: D(lambda) > 0 for all lambda > 1/2 (unrefereed); 0.6039 (refereed)
conditional_on: RH
location: Theorem 2, p. 1; proof in Section 7

history.value: pairs N(0.6039,T) >> N(T) under RH + almost all zeros simple (Thm 4); GRH: 0.5769

caveats: The DPC count includes zero-length spacings, and c_eps may tend to 0, so this is not a positive proportion of gaps <= 1/2. By Conrey-Iwaniec, a positive proportion below 1/2 - eps is exactly what Siegel zeros forbid in their range. The history values before 2020 are taken from Lamzouri's survey paragraph; the original papers were not read.

quantity: lambda: current (2026, unrefereed) record under RH, for zeta and every fixed primitive Dirichlet L-function
statement: Assume RH for L(s,chi), chi a fixed primitive Dirichlet character (conductor Q = 1 is zeta). Then lambda > 3.63846723. Method: a weighted mean of the number of zeros in an interval, with symmetric coefficients c_{m/n} indexed by reduced fractions m/n of squarefree coprime m, n <= Y = sqrt(T)/(log T)^{10}, built from a five-variable polynomial H and prime-factor statistics. The final inequality (8.4) is verified by interval evaluation of finite quadratic forms with margin > 1.0811e-9 at phi = 3.63846723, ell = 1.96635.
conditional_on: RH for L(s,chi) (for zeta: RH)
location: Theorem 3, p. 2; Section 8, eqs. (8.1)-(8.4), pp. 22-24
caveats: Unrefereed. The large-gap part will reportedly appear as a separate rewritten paper. ChatGPT was used to run the large-gap optimizations. The weights are bilinear over rationals, not a single Dirichlet polynomial of length <= T, so this does not contradict the IKT MO limit 3.022. The numerical margin is about 1e-9 (interval arithmetic). The value is below the older CGG/GTT MO threshold 3.6747. The result is compatible with the Alternative Hypothesis.

verification.checked_against: DPC 2610.28527v2 full text: Theorem 3 (p. 2), Sect. 2 overview, Sect. 4 weight definition, Sect. 8 eqs. (8.1)-(8.4) (pp. 20-24), acknowledgements
verification.notes: Confirmed: reduced fractions m/n, squarefree and coprime, m,n <= Y = sqrt(T)/(log T)^{10}; symmetric coefficients from a five-variable polynomial H; ell = 39327/20000; Arb interval evaluation. The margin breaks down as follows: the raw quotient bound is > 2.15088826449e-9, the truncation error (8.3) contributes < 1.069756e-9, and the net margin is > 1.0811e-9. The truncation error bound is therefore load-bearing and about half of the raw margin. The weight is |R_T(t)|^2 with R_T a sum over rational frequencies q^{-it}, so IKT Theorem 3 (integer-indexed f(m)f(km), km <= L) does not literally apply. That supports the ledger's no-contradiction remark, but nobody has proved a matching limitation for DPC's class. Unrefereed. ChatGPT ran the optimizations.

quantity: Largest multiplicity and largest gap (upper bounds)
statement: Assume RH. If 1/2+i gamma is a zero of multiplicity m(gamma), then m(gamma) <= (1/2+o(1)) log gamma/log log gamma. If gamma < gamma' are consecutive ordinates, then gamma'-gamma <= pi(1+o(1))/log log gamma (Goldston-Gonek, Cor. 1). Also under RH |S(t)| <= (1/2+o(1)) log t/log log t (G-G Thm 2), improved to |S(t)| <= (1/4+o(1)) log t/log log t by Carneiro-Chandee-Milinovich. Via m(gamma) <= 2 sup|S| that improvement only reproduces the constant 1/2. Unconditionally, Hall-Hayman: gamma_{n+1}-gamma_n <= (pi/2+o(1))/log log log gamma_n; Littlewood had A/log log log gamma_n with A = 32. Zhao (2025) extends unconditional gap upper bounds to general L-functions. Unconditionally m(gamma) << log gamma (classical).
value: RH: m(gamma) <= (1/2+o(1)) log gamma/loglog gamma; max gap <= (pi+o(1))/loglog gamma. Unconditional: max gap <= (pi/2+o(1))/logloglog gamma.
conditional_on: RH for the multiplicity and loglog gap bounds; Hall-Hayman is unconditional
location: Theorem 1, Theorem 2, Corollary 1 eqs. (9)-(10), p. 2. CCM: arXiv 1503.00955 Theorem 1, p. 1. Hall-Hayman (J. reine angew. Math. 2000) Thm 1 as quoted in Zhao arXiv 2511.13898, eq. (3), p. 1.
caveats: An arXiv search did not find an improvement of the multiplicity constant 1/2 or the gap constant pi under RH, but it was not exhaustive. The conjecture of Ben Arous-Bourgade, quoted in Bui-Milinovich, is limsup (gamma_{n+1}-gamma_n) sqrt(log gamma_n/32) = 1, far below these upper bounds.

The method is mollifier-based, not pair correlation.

caveats: CORRECTION TO THE TASK PROMPT: Bui-Heath-Brown is conditional on RH, not GRH; the extra hypothesis they removed was GLH. Knausgard (2610.08965, p. 2) confirms that 19/27 is still the RH record as of Oct 2026. Unconditional bounds on simple zeros anywhere in the strip reached 0.678 in 2026 (SPACING-SIMP-04), still below 19/27. Gallagher-Mueller (1978): PCC + RH imply 100% simple. quantity: Sum of multiplicities N*(T) = sum m_rho and proportion of distinct zeros (RH, GRH)
statement: Assume RH. Then sum_{0<gamma<=T} m_rho <= (1.3208+o(1)) N(T); under GRH, 1.3155 (Thm 1). Hence (eq. 6) the proportion of simple zeros is >= 0.6792 (RH) or 0.6845 (GRH) (Cor. 2). Combining with Bui-Heath-Brown's 19/27 and Montgomery's identity 2N_s <= N* - 5N + 6N_d gives N_d(T) >= (0.8477+o(1))N(T) under RH and 0.8486 under GRH (Cor. 3). The method replaces bandlimited auxiliary functions by the Cohn-Elkies class (hat f <= 0 for |x| >= 1) and solves the resulting problem by semidefinite programming.

quantity: Unconditional proportion of zeros that are simple AND on the critical line, and of distinct zeros (2026 breakthrough; unrefereed)
statement: Alpoge-Furman, Theorem A, unconditional: N_0^s(T,2T) >= (2/3 - o(1)) N(T,2T) (simple zeros on the line) and N_d(T,2T) >= (5/6 - o(1)) N(T,2T) (distinct zeros). With the Montgomery-Taylor window the constants are 2 - c_MT^{-1} = 0.67250... and (3 - c_MT^{-1})/2 = 0.83625.... The same holds for (0,T) with rate O(log log T/log T). Theorem B: the same for L(s,chi), chi fixed primitive. Mechanism: compress Weil's explicit-formula Hermitian form to d ~ N(T,2T) modulated windows. On-line zeros give rank-one positive parts; off-line pairs give signature-(1,1) blocks (Sylvester inertia). A rank-trace inequality rank P1 >= 2tr P1 + 4tr Q' - 4b - ||P1+Q'||_HS^2 is fed by the unconditional second moment ||G||_HS^2 = (R(psi)+o(1))N, with R(psi0) = 4/3. Later work: Lamzouri (2609.02882) gives a Hilbert-space-inequality proof and adds 'simple or on line' >= 0.88762 and an average of the two proportions >= 0.83625. Wang (2609.24167) adds delta0 = 6.67e-8. Knausgard (2610.08965) proves liminf N_d/N >= 1645064/1960733 = 0.83900459675..., N_s/N >= 0.67800919..., and N_0^s/N >= 1669159/2478195 = 0.67353820....
value: Unconditional: simple and on the line >= 0.67250 (AF; refined to 0.67353820 by Knausgard); distinct >= 0.83625 (AF; 0.83900 by Knausgard); simple anywhere >= 0.67800919 (Knausgard)

distinct 0.8369928 (arXiv 2609.33043), then 0.83900; simple and on the line 0.67353820

caveats: (1) Unrefereed. AF's Theorems A and B are Lean 4-formalized with only the three standard axioms, per the paper's Appendix A; this was not independently re-run here. Knausgard's Lean proofs use three additional axioms, each recording that an external search program returned true, which the Lean kernel does not check. AF's Dirichlet family-average remarks (0.811 and 0.905) are not formalized. (2) Bandwidth-one ceiling: any certificate using only pair correlation with Fourier support [-1,1] cannot exceed about 0.6818 (p0 <= 0.6818287). The Lean check relies on interval enclosures (EnclOK) that are not kernel-checked. AF state that improving on 2/3 materially requires pair-correlation information beyond support 1, and that unconditionally higher trace moments add nothing. (3) Unverified claims: Knausgard lists many unrefereed reports between 0.67300 and 0.673492 (repositories, Zenodo, draft PRs). A Zenodo report by H. Yang and S. Yang claims 0.7962 and 0.8981 from trace moments up to order six, graded by its own authors as having an unverified analytic part. That exceeds the bandwidth-one ceiling and conflicts with AF's 'higher moments add nothing' remark; treat it as unverified. (4) Provenance dispute: AF give the previous unconditional distinct-zero record as 0.6603 (Wu 2015), while Knausgard cites Ki-Lee (Funct. Approx. 47 (2012), Thm 5) for more than 70%; not resolved here. (5) The inputs are insensitive to o(N) off-line zeros and also hold for Davenport-Heilbronn and Epstein zeta functions, where RH fails, so these results give no evidence toward RH.

quantity: Numerical agreement of zeta zeros with GUE statistics (Odlyzko)
statement: Odlyzko's large-scale computations (Math. Comp. 48 (1987) 273-308 near zero #10^12; later near zeros #10^20, #10^22 and #10^23; Contemp. Math. 290 (2001) 139-144) show the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution and pair correlation of normalized zeros agreeing closely with the GUE predictions (Montgomery-Dyson 1-(sin pi u/pi u)^2 and the Gaudin spacing density). They also show small systematic finite-height deviations, e.g. near E = 2.5041178e15, whose amplitude is about 20 times larger than the naive CUE_N correction with N0 = log(E/2pi).
value: Close agreement with GUE at heights up to about 1e22 (zero index about 1e23); finite-height deviations of order 1e-2 in the spacing density
location: Not opened (AMS page blocked by a bot check; Odlyzko's site failed TLS through the proxy). Described from Bogomolny-Bohigas-Leboeuf-Monastra arXiv:math/0602270, Sect. 1 and Fig. 1, and Lagarias-Rodgers ref. [25].
caveats: These floating-point computations are high precision but not interval-certified, so they are not rigorous. They give finite-height evidence only and say nothing about the limiting quantities mu, lambda or simplicity. Separately, Platt-Trudgian (arXiv 2004.09765) verified RH rigorously with interval arithmetic up to height 3,000,175,332,800. Simplicity is not explicitly asserted in the text grepped, so no rigorous simplicity height is recorded here.

Comp. 48 (1987) 273-308, DOI 10.1090/s0025-5718-1987-0866115-0; Platt-Trudgian 2004.09765 full text Theorem 1 and Sect. 2; Crossref: Bull. LMS 53 (2021) 792-797
verification.correction: Optional strengthening of the caveat. Platt-Trudgian Theorem 1 states RH up to 3,000,175,332,800, covering the lowest 12,363,153,437,138 zeros. Their method counts sign changes of the completed zeta function and confirms with Turing's method that this count equals N(T). Matching counts force every zero below that height to be simple. So rigorous simplicity holds to the same height, as a standard consequence the paper does not state explicitly.
verification.notes: Odlyzko's own papers were not opened, so the grade stays secondary. The factor-of-20 statement is confirmed from BBLM.

quantity: Lower-order terms in pair correlation (Bogomolny-Keating) and the finite-height effective matrix size
statement: Bogomolny-Keating (1995-96) conjectured the full pair-correlation density of zeta zeros at finite height, including arithmetic lower-order terms, from Hardy-Littlewood prime-pair heuristics. Bogomolny-Bohigas-Leboeuf-Monastra (2006) argue that to leading order the finite-height deviations of the spacing distribution equal those of CUE matrices of effective dimension N_eff = log(E/2pi)/sqrt(12 Lambda), Lambda = 1.57314..., so N_eff = 0.230158 N0. This matches Odlyzko's data near E = 2.504e15, with residual structure attributed to O(N_eff^{-4}) terms. Rigorous partial confirmation: under RH, for sufficiently smooth test functions with restricted Fourier support, the Bogomolny-Keating measure matches the true pair-correlation measure up to a very small error (Rodgers 2013). Conrey-Snaith (2008) derive all lower-order terms of n-correlation from the Conrey-Farmer-Zirnbauer ratios conjecture.
value: N_eff = log(E/2pi)/sqrt(12*1.57314...) (heuristic); BK measure confirmed under RH only for restricted smooth test functions
conditional_on: Hardy-Littlewood conjectures (BK); ratios conjecture (Conrey-Snaith); RH and restricted test functions (Rodgers)
location: Abstract and eq. (19), p. 1 and p. 7; comparison with Odlyzko data, Fig. 2 and Sect. 4

history.value: conjectural finite-T pair correlation with arithmetic terms
second main terms in the Goldston-Montgomery equivalence (RH + twin-prime-type hypothesis)
all lower-order terms from the ratios conjecture
BK measure confirmed under RH for restricted smooth test functions

caveats: Bogomolny-Keating and BBLM are heuristic or physical arguments. Only Rodgers' restricted-support statement is a theorem (conditional on RH). The BK and Conrey-Snaith papers were not opened here.

quantity: Largest height H to which RH for zeta is verified by a rigorous (interval/ball-arithmetic) refereed computation
statement: Unconditional, rigorous computation. Every nontrivial zero beta+i*gamma of zeta(s) with 0<gamma<=3,000,175,332,800 has beta=1/2. Equivalently, the lowest 12,363,153,437,138 nontrivial zeros lie on Re s=1/2. Method: Platt's windowed Booker/FFT evaluation of the completed zeta function on the half-line, reimplemented in Arb ball arithmetic in place of MPFI. On-line zeros are counted from sign changes. Completeness comes from Turing's method in Trudgian's 2011 and 2016 versions. No zero was isolated beyond detecting its sign change. About 7.5 million core hours on 3.6 GHz Xeons; sampling about 25 points per zero.
location: Theorem 1, p.2 of arXiv v1; computational details in Section 2, pp.2-3; Corollary 2 (Lambda<=0.2) in Section 3.4, p.5

history.authors: van de Lune, te Riele, Winter
history.note: refereed, classical floating-point error analysis (see VERIF-06)
first interval-arithmetic verification at this scale (VERIF-02)
about 98x Platt 2017 and about 5500x the 1986 height; 22% above Gourdon's unrefereed H

caveats: (1) Theorem 1 asserts beta=1/2 only. It does not state that the zeros are simple; rigorous simplicity is stated only up to 3.06e10 (VERIF-02). (2) The zbMATH review (Zbl 1482.11111) notes that no permanent link to the code is given. (3) I found no independent rigorous replication as of 2026-11-17. The authors say it independently confirms the non-rigorous results of Gourdon, Wedeniwski and Franke et al. (4) Rigor is relative to correct implementation, hardware and compiler. No certificate exists that is cheaper to check than the computation itself (Gourdon 2004, Section 1.1). (5) Searches (arXiv API, zbMATH, web) found no larger rigorous H published 2021-2026. This is a search result, not proof that none exists. (6) Applications: Corollary 2 gives Lambda<=0.2 using Polymath15 Table 1 (needs H>2.51e12). Johnston (arXiv 2109.02249) derives explicit prime-counting bounds from this H.

source.title: The Riemann hypothesis is true up to 3*10^12

verification.checked_against: arXiv 2004.09765 full text (Theorem 1, Section 2, Section 3.4 Corollary 2, footnote 1); Crossref DOI 10.1112/blms.12460 (BLMS 53(3) 792-797, online 22 Jan 2021); zbMATH Zbl 1482.11111 review (Balazard)
verification.notes: Verbatim matches: 'The Riemann hypothesis is true up to height 3 000 175 332 800. That is, the lowest 12 363 153 437 138 non-trivial zeroes have Re rho = 1/2'. Also confirmed: Arb ball arithmetic replaced MPFI; about 7.5 million core hours on 3.6 GHz Xeons; about 110,000 of half-line per GHz-hour; Gourdon's run '725 times quicker', attributed to 25 samples per zero versus 1.2 and to multiprecision rigorous numerics. Also confirmed: '22% higher' than the earlier claims, the Corollary 2 bound Lambda<=0.2 via Polymath15 Table 1 (H>2.51e12), and the zbMATH remark that no permanent code link is given. Two details to add. First, the sampling rate 'isolated 999 997.5 out of every 1 000 000 zeroes', which supports the caveat that simplicity is not certified. Second, the x<=2.169e25 range is Platt-Trudgian's own Corollary 1, obtained via Buethe Section 7. Completeness uses the integrated-S(t) bound of Trudgian [34,35], not the Lehman-Brent Gram-block corollary. So the factor-2 error that Amberger (arXiv 2512.23064) alleges in the Gram-block count K does not obviously touch this result.

quantity: Rigorously isolated zeros of zeta to high precision (and certified simplicity)
statement: Every nontrivial zero rho with |Im rho|<=3.0610046e10 is simple and has Re rho=1/2. The 103,800,788,359 zeros with 0<Im s<30,610,046,000 were isolated to absolute precision +-2^-102 using about 6e12 high-precision evaluations (MPFI, 300-bit working precision) of a windowed Booker/Odlyzko-Schoenhage-type FFT algorithm. Completeness comes from Turing's method with Trudgian's Theorem 2.2. The ordinates (1.3 TB) are distributed through the LMFDB.
location: Theorem 5.1 and the paragraph before it, Section 5 (p.~10 of the Bristol author-accepted manuscript); error bounds in Appendix A
caveats: Read from the Bristol author-accepted manuscript (research-information.bris.ac.uk), not the AMS version of record. Tao (arXiv 1201.6656, proof of Theorem 1.5) cites this H as 3.06e10 and deliberately uses the more conservative T0=3.29e9, which he describes as checked by four independent computations. This is the only rigorous dataset of individually located zeros at this scale. Platt-Trudgian 2021 did not store or refine zeros.

quantity: Gourdon's floating-point verification of the first 10^13 zeros (unrefereed)
statement: Unrefereed preprint, not interval arithmetic. Using an optimized Odlyzko-Schoenhage algorithm in hardware floating point with explicit error bounds (Turing's method with the bound int S <= 2.30+0.128 log(t2/2pi)), the first 10^13 nontrivial zeros were found to lie on the critical line; Platt-Trudgian and Tao give H about 2.44e12. The run took the equivalent of 525 days of a 2.4 GHz Pentium 4 in 2003, averaged 1.193 evaluations of Z per zero, and was checked by sampling Riemann-Siegel values against Odlyzko-Schoenhage output and by a full rerun with different parameters. The same paper reports 2 billion zeros at each height 10^n for 13<=n<=24, including from the 10^24-th zero.
value: 10^13 zeros; H about 2.44e12
location: Section 3 (pp.19-25), Section 3.3.1 'Computation information' p.22; history table p.2; Section 4 p.25

history.value: 250e9 zeros per Gourdon's table (heights disputed, see VERIF-04)

caveats: (1) Never published in a refereed journal. Platt-Trudgian 2021 (p.2) say it is 'not clear how the computations were set up to avoid problematic accumulation of rounding and truncation errors', citing concerns by Tao and Helfgott. Superseded rigorously by VERIF-01. (2) Gourdon himself notes that verification costs as much as the computation and that such results are hard to regard as 'proved' in the strong sense (Section 1.1). (3) The Gram-block and Rosser statistics in the same paper are described there as 'not completely rigorous', because Gram points with undecidable sign were perturbed. (4) The paper's Turing bound 2.30+0.128 log(t/2pi) equals about 2.065+0.128 log t, consistent with Turing's triple (2.07, 0.128) as cited by Trudgian 2011.

statement: Distributed computation (ZetaGrid, 2001-2005) using plain Riemann-Siegel; unrefereed. Platt-Trudgian document inconsistent claims. A Wikipedia link gives 900 billion (the frequently quoted H=2.41e11). Franke, Kleinjung, Buethe and Jost (Math. Comp. 86 (2017)) claim H=10^11 with few computational details.

quantity: Brent 1979 verification (H(75,000,001)) and the early verification ladder
statement: Brent (1979): zeta(s) has exactly 75,000,000 zeros with 0<t<32,585,736.4; all are simple and on sigma=1/2, so H(75,000,001) holds. The method is Lehmer-style Riemann-Siegel evaluation with Gram blocks, Rosser's rule and Turing's theorem. Brent's introduction lists earlier results: Gram H(10), Backlund H(79), Hutchinson H(138) and Titchmarsh-Comrie H(1,041) by hand; then Lehmer H(25,000) on a digital computer, Meller H(35,337), Lehman H(250,000), and Rosser-Yohe-Schoenfeld H(3,500,000). Table 3 lists all 15 exceptions to Rosser's rule up to Gram block B_75,000,000, the first at n=13,999,525.
location: Abstract and Section 1, p.1361; Tables 2-4, pp.1369-1370; reference list p.1372 (scanned PDF from the author's site, pages viewed as images)

history.value: H(10) per Brent; 15 zeros located per Gourdon/Trudgian
H(138) (t<=300); found the first Gram's-law failure at g_125/g_126
1,104 zeros (Gourdon table); also checked the window 2pi*63^2<t<2pi*64^2

caveats: Discrepancies. (a) Gourdon's 2004 table lists Brent 1979 as 81,000,001 zeros (and 1977 as 40,000,000), but the 1979 paper itself states H(75,000,001). The 81,000,001 figure may be a later extension; not verified. (b) Gram is H(10) (Brent) versus 15 zeros located (Gourdon, Trudgian). (c) Bober-Hiary (arXiv 1607.00709, footnote 1) note that Titchmarsh stated there are 1041 zeros in 0<t<1468, whereas there are 1042. (d) Errata exist for Rosser-Yohe-Schoenfeld 1969 (Math. Comp. 29 (1975) p.243, cited in Brent's reference 23). (e) Turing's 1953 paper 'contains several errors' that Lehman (1970) corrected (Trudgian 2011, p.2). (f) 'Rigorous' here means classical floating-point error analysis, not interval arithmetic.

quantity: Explicit constants in Turing's method for zeta: |int_{t1}^{t2} S(t) dt| <= a + b log t2 (+ c log log t2)
statement: Unconditional theorems. Trudgian 2011, Theorem 2.2: for t2>t1>168*pi, |int_{t1}^{t2} S(t)dt| <= 2.067+0.059 log t2. Corollary 2.3: if N consecutive Gram blocks with union [g_n,g_p) satisfy Rosser's rule and N >= 0.0031 log^2 g_p + 0.11 log g_p, then N(g_n)<=n+1 and N(g_p)>=p+1, so at g_p=2pi*10^12 only 6 Rosser blocks are needed. Trudgian 2016, Theorem 1: for t2>t1>10^5, |int S| <= 1.698+0.183 log log t2+0.049 log t2, with height-optimized triples in Table 1.
location: Theorem 2.2 and Corollary 2.3, pp.3-4 (arXiv v3); sequel: Trudgian, Improvements to Turing's method II, Rocky Mountain J. Math. 46 (2016) 325-332, arXiv 1406.3416, Theorem 1 p.1 and Table 1 p.6

history.note: paper contains errors, corrected by Lehman

caveats: Trudgian 2011 footnote 3: the constant 168pi in Turing's and Lehman's triples 'seems to be a misprint'; their arguments only need t>128pi. Trudgian 2011 (p.~16) reports that the minimal b attainable by his method is 0.0353. Trudgian 2016, Section 4: 'it seems difficult to improve substantially on Theorem 1'; the most promising target is the log 4 term from Booker's Lemma 4.4. Bober-Hiary and Gourdon quote the older 2.30+0.128 log(t/2pi), which is equivalent to Turing's constants.

source.title: Improvements to Turing's method

verification.checked_against: arXiv 0903.1885v3 (Trudgian 2011) Theorem 2.2, Corollary 2.3, footnote 3, Section 2.3; arXiv 1406.3416 (Trudgian 2016) Theorem 1, Table 1, Section 4; arXiv 2512.23064v3 (Amberger, 4 Jan 2026) Theorems 2.1 and 2.3, Table 3, Remark 5.1
verification.correction: Trudgian's constants are confirmed as stated: (2.067, 0.059) for t2>t1>168pi, and 1.698+0.183 loglog t2+0.049 log t2 for t2>t1>10^5. However, an unrefereed preprint, V. S. G. Amberger, 'Bounding the integral of the argument of the Riemann zeta function' (arXiv 2512.23064, v3 Jan 2026), makes two claims. (i) Theorem 2.1: |S1(t2)-S1(t1)| <= 1.680+0.186 log log t2+0.0314 log t2 for t2>t1>=653, optimized near 1e12. Remark 5.1 gives the variant 3.355+0.160 loglog+0.018 log. This beats Trudgian's Table 1 at every tabulated height, and its c is below the 0.0353 floor of Trudgian's 2011 method. It uses second-log-derivative contributions and the Hiary-Patel-Yang zeta bounds. (ii) A 'minor mistake in Lehman's argument' makes the Lehman-Brent lower bound on the number K of Rosser-satisfying Gram blocks off by a factor of 2. Amberger says the same error is in Brent's and Trudgian's estimates, so Corollary 2.3 and its claim that 'only 6 Gram blocks' suffice at 2pi*10^12 are affected. His corrected Theorem 2.3 needs 9 blocks at heights <=3.6e12, 8 at <=3.6e11 and 7 at <=3.2e10. Both claims are unrefereed and should be carried as such.
verification.notes: Minor location fix: the 0.0353 floor is in Section 2.3 (about p.10 of arXiv v3), not p.16. Labeling is inconsistent: the quantity field writes a+b log t2 (+c log log t2), while the value field uses Trudgian 2016's ordering, in which b is the loglog coefficient and c the log coefficient.

quantity: Completeness and verification methods other than Turing's (explicit formula; Riemann's Hadamard-product method)
statement: Hiary-Ireland-Kyi develop Riemann's verification idea (Hadamard product plus positivity and one evaluation of a logarithmic derivative in the region of absolute convergence) into theorems (Theorems 7, 11, 13) that certify RH and list-completeness in a window [y-eta, y+eta], given intervals containing sign changes. Numerical example: around y=10^28+501675.8 with tau=501575.4, Theorem 13(i) verified RH in a window of eta=70216 containing 1,399,910 zeros, and Theorem 13(iii) certified completeness for eta=49650 (989,881 zeros). This is conditional on the input zero ordinates being accurate to +-10^-10. Buethe (2015) gives an explicit-formula (Weil-Barner) completeness test that sacrifices asymptotically fewer zeros than Turing's method. It applies to an extension of the Selberg class and is specialized to Hecke L-series and elliptic-curve L-functions.
value: window at t about 1e28: 1,399,910 zeros (eta = 70216)
conditional_on: Correctness of the input zero lists from the LMFDB and the paper's [Zet] reference, to +-10^-10. The interval arithmetic was done in mpmath. Riemann-Siegel or LCALC data are assumed accurate to +-10^-8.
location: Theorems 11 and 13 (Section 6); Section 7.1 numerical example, pp.17-18 of arXiv v1. Buethe: Math. Comp. 84 (2015) 2413-2431, arXiv 1308.6704, abstract only.

quantity: Complexity exponent for evaluating zeta(1/2+it) to +-t^{-lambda}
statement: Unconditional theorem (algorithmic). For any fixed lambda, zeta(1/2+it) can be computed to within +-t^{-lambda} using at most A1 (log t)^kappa1 t^{4/13} operations on numbers of at most A2 (log t)^2 bits. This requires a one-time precomputation of at most A3 (log t)^kappa2 t^{4/13} operations and at most A4 (log t)^kappa3 t^{4/13} bits of storage. With little storage, the exponent is 1/3 (Hiary, quadratic exponential sums). Amortized: Hiary's elementary method evaluates zeta at any floor(T^{1/4}) points of [T, T+T^{1/4}] in average time T^{1/4+o(1)} per point. Odlyzko-Schoenhage (1988) computes about T^{1/2} values in time T^{1/2+eps}, so verification to height H costs about H^{1+o(1)}.
value: single point: t^{4/13+o(1)} (about t^0.3077); little-space: t^{1/3+o(1)}
location: Theorem 1.1, p.2 (arXiv v4); amortized method: Hiary, Math. Comp. 80 (2011) 1785-1796, arXiv 1002.2443, abstract
caveats: Disputed exponent: the zbMATH review (Zbl 1243.11118) states the main result with t^{3/14} operations and storage, and says 3/14 is smaller than current bounds for mu(1/2). Every arXiv version (v1-v4, which I checked) and Bober-Hiary 2018 state 4/13. I treat 4/13 as correct and the review's 3/14 as an apparent reviewer error. I did not see the Annals version of record. No published 2011-2026 improvement of 4/13 was found. A faster single-point algorithm does not reduce the cost of full verification, which is dominated by the about H log H zeros.

quantity: Theorems on Gram's law, the Weak Gram law and Rosser's rule (infinitely often / positive proportion)
statement: Unconditional theorems. For sufficiently large T, a positive proportion of the Gram intervals (g_n, g_{n+1}] in [T,2T] contain no zero of zeta(1/2+it). Hence Gram's law (exactly one zero per Gram interval) and the Weak Gram law (at least one zero) both fail for a positive proportion of intervals. A positive proportion of Gram intervals in [T,2T] contain at least one zero, so the Weak Gram law succeeds a positive proportion of the time. Earlier: Titchmarsh proved that Gram's law fails infinitely often and that the Weak Gram law holds infinitely often; Lehman (1970) first showed that Rosser's rule fails infinitely often.
value: positive proportion of failures (Gram, Weak Gram) and of successes (Weak Gram); constants not explicit
location: arXiv 0811.0883: Theorem 1 (p.5), Theorem 2 (p.6), Theorem 3 (p.9); published statement per the zbMATH review Zbl 1281.11084

history.value: Gram's law fails infinitely often; Weak Gram law holds infinitely often

caveats: Read in the 2008 arXiv preprint; the published Acta Arith. version was checked only through zbMATH. Hanga-Hughes (arXiv 1911.03190, p.2) state that it is still unproven whether the strong Gram's law is true infinitely often, let alone for a positive proportion. Hanga-Hughes cite the journal as 'Acta Arith. 143', but zbMATH gives volume 148. Related work: Korolev (arXiv 1011.3997) proves several of Selberg's unproved 1946 formulae on Gram's law.

verification.notes: The arXiv v1 (2008) proves positive-proportion failures of Gram's law (Theorem 1) and of the Weak Gram law (Theorem 2, via N_F0/N_g >= A/2), and positive-proportion successes of the Weak Gram law (Theorem 3). It contains no Rosser-rule theorem. The published title adds 'and the Rosser Rule', and the zbMATH review says the paper treats the Rosser rule for infinitely many intervals and positive proportion. I could not check whether the published version proves a positive-proportion Rosser-rule failure. If it does, the negative-results section should cite it rather than only Lehman 1970's 'infinitely often'. The Hanga-Hughes statement that the strong Gram law is not known to hold infinitely often is confirmed as their claim (2019).

statement: Rigorous computation (double-precision interval arithmetic via SSE2, plus MPFI where needed; Turing's method after Booker, Rumely and Trudgian). GRH holds for all Dirichlet L-functions of primitive characters with modulus q<=400,000, up to height t0 = max(10^8/q, 7.5*10^7/q + 200) for even q and t0 = max(10^8/q, 3.75*10^7/q + 200) for odd q. This covers 29,565,923,837 L-functions and about 3.8e13 zeros in about 400,000 core hours. Also Theorem 7.2: L_chi(1/2) != 0 for every primitive chi with q<=2,000,000 (739,151,526,102 characters).

location: Theorem 7.1 and Theorem 7.2, Section 7 'Results', pp.14-15 (arXiv v1)

quantity: Computational exclusion of real (Landau-Siegel) zeros of quadratic Dirichlet L-functions
statement: Rigorous computation (FLINT plus Arb ball arithmetic, about 150,000 core hours). This is a zero-free interval on the real axis, not full GRH: Platt (2016) gives L(sigma,chi) != 0 for all sigma>0 for q<=4e5, and Watkins (2004) for odd chi with q<=3e8.

statement: Rigorous computations (MPFI interval arithmetic). (a) Booker 2006: RH tested for Dedekind zeta functions of a few S5 and A5 number fields in |Im s| <= 100, together with Artin's conjecture for all S5 representations in the same region. (b) Booker-Then 2018, Theorem 8.2: for each of the first 2191 Maass cusp forms on SL(2,Z), i.e. spectral parameter 0<=r<=178, all nontrivial zeros of the L-function with 0<=t<=30000 are simple and on the critical line; each list has more than 60,000 consecutive zeros. This also makes Cho's simple-zero theorem unconditional. (c) Booker-Platt 2019, Corollary 1.2: the Selberg zeta function of PSL(2,Z)\H has exactly 2,184 zeros with imaginary part in (0, 177.75], all simple, via Turing's method for Selberg zeta (Theorem 1.1). (d) The LMFDB zeta-zero database is Platt's rigorous +-2^-102 data (VERIF-02).

quantity: Uniform zero-density exponent sup_{1/2≤σ<1} A(σ) for ζ(s)
statement: Unconditionally, for every fixed σ ∈ [1/2,1] and every ε>0, N(σ,T) ≪_{σ,ε} T^{(30/13)(1−σ)+ε} as T→∞. GM Theorem 1.2 gives A(σ) ≤ 15/(3+5σ) for every σ. verification.correction: The headline is correct: sup A ≤ 30/13, attained at σ = 7/10, and GM's §13.1 proof structure is as described. The history is wrong, though. Ingham 1940's 3/(2−σ) was never the uniform record. Ingham 1937 already gave A ≤ 2+4c, which is 8/3 with c = 1/6, and that is the source of θ > 5/8. Montgomery 1969 gave min(3/(2−σ), 2/σ), whose supremum is 5/2 at σ = 4/5; that is the source of θ > 3/5 and of the 5/2 that CGL cite. The corrected sequence is 4 (Carlson 1921) → about 8/3 (Ingham 1937) → 5/2 (Montgomery 1969) → 12/5 (Huxley 1972) → 30/13 (GM). The ledger's own ZDE-08 history (5/8, 3/5) and ZDE-15 (the '8/3 shape' of Ingham 1937) contradict '4 → 3 → 12/5'. Separately, the caveat 'ineffective' is wrong. GM's argument has no ineffective step (there is no Siegel-zero issue); the bound is effective but not explicit.
verification.notes: I confirmed the GM acknowledgement text: 'thank the anonymous referees for a number of helpful comments and corrections'. GM state Theorem 1.2 with no σ restriction; the proof combines Ingham (σ ≤ 7/10), Huxley (σ ≥ 8/10), and Theorem 1.1 or the MVT applied to D^k (13.1–13.2). In §13.2 the log factor appears only as (log T)^{O(1)} in (13.3).

quantity: Guth–Maynard large-values estimate for Dirichlet polynomials
statement: Hypotheses: |b_n| ≤ 1 (an ℓ∞ bound), (t_r)_{r≤R} 1-separated in [0,T], and |Σ_{n=N}^{2N} b_n n^{it_r}| ≥ V for every r. Conclusion: R ≤ T^{o(1)}(N^2V^{−2} + N^{18/5}V^{−4} + T N^{12/5}V^{−4}). This beats the classical MVT + Montgomery–Halász–Huxley bound R ≤ T^{o(1)}(N^2V^{−2} + T·min(NV^{−2}, N^4V^{−6})) exactly when N^{7/10+ε} < V < N^{8/10−ε} and N ≤ T^{5/6−ε}. In the key case N = T^{4/5}, V = N^{3/4} it gives R ≤ T^{13/25+o(1)} instead of T^{3/5}. The core result is Proposition 3.1: |W| ≤ T N^{(12−20σ)/5+o(1)} for W in an interval of length T = N^{6/5}. Larger T are reached by Huxley subdivision. Proposition 12.1 refines the bound for N ≥ T^{5/6}: R ⪅ N^{2−2σ} + T^{1/2}N^{3−4σ} + T^{(30σ−21)/5}N^{(46−60σ)/5}.
value: R ⪅ N^2V^{−2} + N^{18/5}V^{−4} + T N^{12/5}V^{−4}. At σ = 3/4, T = N^{6/5}: |W| ⪅ N^{0.6}, against N^{0.7} from the MVT and N^{0.5} conjectured (Montgomery).
location: Theorem 1.1, p. 1; Proposition 3.1, p. 9; master inequality (12.1) and Proposition 12.1, pp. 46–47 (arXiv v2)

caveats: The ℓ∞ hypothesis is essential to the method (GM Remark, p. 5). Cossaboom (arXiv 2609.27715, unrefereed) relaxes it to ℓ^q with q ≥ 8/3. Guth's survey (arXiv 2503.07410, §6) reports that Diakonikolas–Hopkins–Pensia–Tiegel independently get the same shape, N^{3−4σ}T^{1/2}, for random Gaussian matrices for all N ≤ T ≤ N^2. For Dirichlet polynomials GM obtain that shape only at T ≈ N^{6/5} and pass to larger T by subdivision, which costs a full factor T/N^{6/5}.

quantity: Zero-density exponent for the family of Dirichlet L-functions mod q, uniform in q and T
statement: Theorem 1.2: Σ_{χ mod q} N(σ,T,χ) ≤ (qT)^{o(1)}(q^{7(1−σ)/3}T^{2(1−σ)} + (qT)^{30(1−σ)/13}). Hence the uniform exponent is A = 7/3. If q is T-smooth the exponent is 30/13. Finer bounds are available through a divisor q_1 | q. The large-values input (Theorem 1.1) holds for N ≥ (qT)^{2/3}: |W| ≤ (qT)^{o(1)}(N^2V^{−2} + (qT)^{1/2}N^3V^{−4} + q^{4/3}TN^2V^{−4} + qTN^{12/5}V^{−4}). Applications: the least Goldbach number in a residue class mod a prime p is ≪ p^{7/6+ε}, and asymptotics for primes in arithmetic progressions in short intervals (prime-power moduli, h/φ(q) ≥ x^{17/30+ε}).
value: A = 7/3 ≈ 2.333 uniformly (previously 12/5); 30/13 for T-smooth q
location: Theorem 1.1, pp. 1–2; Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3, p. 3; Corollaries 1.4–1.5, p. 4 (arXiv v2)

Shparlinski suggests the Linnik constant for prime-power moduli (currently 2.1115) could be improved; CGL do not pursue this.

quantity: Negative results and barriers for the large-values route to zero density
statement: (i) A(1/2) = 2 by Riemann–von Mangoldt (TTY eq. (27)), so the DH exponent 2 is optimal at σ = 1/2. (ii) LV(σ,τ) ≥ min(2−2σ, τ) (TTY Lemma 29; GM footnote 1 constructs |W| ≫ N^{2−2σ}), so Montgomery's large-values conjecture is sharp. (iii) Bourgain's counterexample to Montgomery's original ℓ2-normalised conjecture (GM p. 4; Guth §3.4). (iv) Bourgain: Montgomery's ℓq large-values conjecture implies the 'Bourgain–Kakeya' conjecture for fat arithmetic progressions, which implies the Kakeya conjecture in every dimension (Guth survey §9, p. 39). Guth notes that assuming Bourgain–Kakeya as a black box currently gives no LV improvement. (v) Partial converse (Matomäki–Teräväinen 2024; TTY Lemma 40): zero-density bounds imply ζ-large-value bounds, so better A(σ) cannot bypass LV_ζ. (vi) Computational barrier: for planted large-value problems, low-degree tests cannot beat the operator-norm bound in a parameter range (Mao–Wein, per Guth §8). There is no meaningful numerical evidence for the LV conjectures even at N = 200 (Guth §4).
value: Floors: A(1/2) = 2 and LV ≥ min(2−2σ, τ); DH via the ℓq LV conjecture is at least as hard as Kakeya in all dimensions
location: Guth §3.4–3.5 (pp. ~10–12), §4 (p. ~13), §9 (pp. 37–40, Conjecture 9.3 and Bourgain's implication on p. 39). TTY Lemma 29 (p. 16) and Lemma 40 (p. 25).

history.value: counterexample to the ℓ2 Montgomery conjecture; Kakeya connection

caveats: Items (iv) and (vi) are barriers to proof strategies, not impossibility theorems for A(σ). (vi) depends on the low-degree conjecture. Maier-type results cap short-interval applications regardless of A: the PNT fails at y = (log x)^A (Gafni–Tao §1.1).
